section_summary: This section examines Japan’s capacity to finance rising naval and military expenditure through budgets, taxes, and bond issues. It includes balance-of-payments analysis, embassy reporting on fiscal policy after the February 1936 uprising, and exchanges about a British article questioning Japan’s economic outlook. The final pages contain repeated copies of a September 1936 embassy assessment of debt, bond absorption, and inflation risks.

subfiles.title: Study of Japan’s economic capacity and international balance of payments
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan’s domestic economy and external accounts could sustain heavy additional expenditure.
subfiles.summary: Production indices and balance-of-payments tables cover 1925–1934. The analysis notes a shrinking trade deficit, positive invisible receipts, capital outflow, and earlier specie exports. It concludes that neither Japan’s internal finances nor its external position presents an immediate obstacle to continued heavy spending.

subfiles.title: Checks on Kawakami’s economic comparisons
subfiles.about: Checks Kawakami’s comparisons of national debt, taxation, and exports against published and Treasury sources.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages compare Japanese and U.S. debt figures, question the reliability of tax-to-income estimates, and tabulate export declines across several countries.

subfiles.title: Breaking point
subfiles.about: Reproduces Kawakami’s claim that Japan could finance naval competition if it arose.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes the closing exchange of Kawakami’s Washington Post article, including claims about income, trade, debt, taxation, and exports used to argue that Japan could meet naval-building costs.

subfiles.title: Japanese fiscal situation and competitive naval building
subfiles.about: Summarizes a study of Japan’s ability to bear the costs of competitive naval building.
subfiles.summary: The adviser judges that Japan could probably carry likely costs for two to five years through rising debt, though longer continuation would cause severe fiscal strain. The memorandum notes the finance minister’s resignation and expects banks to absorb new bonds.

subfiles.title: Principal economic statistics—Japan and United States
subfiles.about: Compares national wealth, debt, budgets, and population for Japan and the United States.
subfiles.summary: A two-page table converts Japanese figures at par and current exchange rates and lists sources for each comparison.

subfiles.title: Thirty-Fourth Financial and Economic Annual of Japan
subfiles.about: Records an annual issued by Japan’s Department of Finance and filed separately.
subfiles.summary: Notes that one copy of the 1934 annual was filed in overflow.

subfiles.title: Export trade and Japan’s internal economic situation
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on exports and a budget strained by defense spending.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 1206 and notes defense spending approaching half the 1935–36 budget.

subfiles.title: Possible British loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a conversation about possible British loans to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a Moscow conversation and proposed notice to the Soviet government of future British loans.

subfiles.title: Government finance: general improvement
subfiles.about: Points to despatch 1304 on improvements in Japanese government finance.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a report of general improvement in government finance.

subfiles.title: Government finance and economic conditions
subfiles.about: Reports official confidence in foreign payments and reviews April trade and financial trends.
subfiles.summary: Finance officials express confidence about foreign commitments and Japan’s international accounts. The extract also discusses Latin American import plans, April’s trade deficit, interest rates, securities markets, and the yen-dollar rate.

subfiles.title: Premier’s statement on defense expenditures
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch containing Premier Okada’s statement on defense spending.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 1387 and Okada’s refusal to reduce defense spending.

subfiles.title: Premier Okada on national defense expenditures
subfiles.about: Quotes Premier Okada saying defense expenditure cannot be reduced.
subfiles.summary: Okada says national security makes cuts to defense expenditure impossible.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Japanese government bonds
subfiles.about: Points to correspondence requesting current values of Japanese government bonds.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Woodruff’s transmission of Herman Dehnke’s bond list and valuation request.

subfiles.title: Government finance
subfiles.about: Points to despatch 1427 on government finance.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a despatch on the forthcoming budget and bond policy.

subfiles.title: Budget demands and deficit bonds
subfiles.about: Reports projected 1936–37 budget demands and Takahashi’s warnings about deficit bonds.
subfiles.summary: Expected ministry demands greatly exceed the current budget. Finance Minister Takahashi warns against indefinite deficit-bond issuance but appears unlikely to curb Army and Navy demands substantially.

subfiles.title: Reduction of ministry budget demands
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on ministry cooperation with budget reductions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 1475 on efforts to reduce 1936–37 budget demands.

subfiles.title: Finance Ministry efforts to limit the 1936–37 budget
subfiles.about: Reports Takahashi’s budget ceiling and the ministries’ submitted demands.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi seeks to hold the budget near the previous year’s level while Army and Navy demands remain high.

subfiles.title: Thirty-Fifth Financial and Economic Annual of Japan
subfiles.about: Records a two-volume Japanese financial annual filed separately.
subfiles.summary: Notes that the 1935 annual’s two volumes were filed in overflow.

subfiles.title: Financial conditions after the Tokyo uprising
subfiles.about: Reports business disruption but financial stability after the February uprising.
subfiles.summary: Exchanges and clearing houses closed temporarily, but banks showed no panic and the Bank of Japan met funding needs. Grew warns that a sharp change in financial policy by the new cabinet could unsettle bond operations.

subfiles.title: Authority of diplomats to borrow for governments
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum on diplomatic borrowing authority and repayment liability.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references legal comments on whether an ambassador or embassy chancellor may borrow without special authority.

subfiles.title: Takahashi on taxation and the national budget
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on taxation, the 1936–37 budget, and bond absorption.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 1693 and statements by Takahashi and financial leaders.

subfiles.title: Government finance and the 1936–37 budget
subfiles.about: Reports Takahashi’s budget speech and differing views of future bond absorption.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi presents a balanced 1936–37 budget and rejects an immediate tax rise after the naval conference. Seinosuke Gō warns that government bonds may become harder to place; Bank of Japan governor Fukai expresses greater confidence.

subfiles.title: Japanese budget for fiscal year 1936–37
subfiles.about: Transmits an ordinance carrying the previous year’s budget into 1936–37.
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that no ordinary detailed annual budget will be available unless a supplementary budget is formulated.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 29
subfiles.about: Carries the previous fiscal year’s budget into fiscal 1936–37.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance invokes Article 71 of the Constitution to continue the previous budget.

subfiles.title: Government finances and proposed policy changes
subfiles.about: Points to a report on higher taxes, defense spending, and other fiscal measures.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 1781 on the new government’s financial plans.

subfiles.title: Baba’s fiscal plans and March financial trends
subfiles.about: Describes Baba’s proposed fiscal changes and Japan’s trade and market conditions.
subfiles.summary: Baba proposes gradual increases in spending and taxation while continuing deficit bonds. Vice Minister Kawagoe links reform to longstanding economic grievances and expects the yen-dollar policy to continue. The extract also records March trade deficits and weak securities markets.

subfiles.title: Comment on ‘Japan in Suspense’
subfiles.about: Checks a British article’s figures against Japanese data and adds trade figures.
subfiles.summary: The division finds the marked claims accurate and notes that export growth was leveling off while imports continued to rise.

subfiles.title: Article concerning the Japanese economic situation
subfiles.about: Transmits the Statist article ‘Japan in Suspense.’
subfiles.summary: Atherton forwards the June 20 article for the Department’s consideration.

subfiles.title: Japan in Suspense
subfiles.about: Argues that armament spending, slowing exports, and weak civilian demand place Japan’s economy under strain.
subfiles.summary: The article contrasts an expanding armament boom with weaker export growth, rising imports, and declining real wages. It anticipates greater bond borrowing and possible inflation while describing the government’s difficulty funding both defense and social relief. It presents retrenchment and expansionary spending as competing policy paths.

subfiles.title: Request for Commerce comment on ‘Japan in Suspense’
subfiles.about: Requests comment on the article forwarded from London.
subfiles.summary: Encloses despatch 2288 and asks Commerce for its assessment.

subfiles.title: Request for Tokyo embassy comment on ‘Japan in Suspense’
subfiles.about: Requests the ambassador’s comment on the article forwarded from London.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the article and asks the Tokyo embassy for its assessment.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department comment on ‘Japan in Suspense’
subfiles.about: Questions the article’s pessimism while acknowledging risks from bonds and future export limits.
subfiles.summary: Commerce argues that gains in other exports offset some textile declines and that wool accounts for much of the import increase. It distinguishes wage rates from earnings, cites improved farm purchasing power, and quotes Trade Commissioner Steintorf’s generally favorable current assessment with reservations about future deficit bonds and export markets.

subfiles.title: Financial position of Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan can finance defense expansion and social reform through additional bonds.
subfiles.summary: Dickover reviews rising national debt, projected 1937–38 deficits, and competing claims about how many bonds Japan can absorb. Foreign bankers doubt that all new capital will be available for government bonds because of investments elsewhere and debt obligations. He concludes that forced bond placement could fund both military expansion and reforms, but would risk inflation and yen depreciation.

subfiles.title: Financial position of Japan—duplicate copy
subfiles.about: Repeats the embassy assessment of Japan’s debt, defense budget, and bond capacity.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats despatch 2038’s estimates of debt and forthcoming deficits. It weighs finance minister Baba’s bond-absorption limit against military demands and describes the inflation and exchange-rate risks of compulsory bond placement.

subfiles.title: Financial position of Japan—further duplicate copy
subfiles.about: Repeats the same embassy assessment of Japan’s fiscal outlook.
subfiles.summary: A further copy of despatch 2038 reviews debt, future defense costs, limits on bond absorption, and the risk of inflation if bonds are forcibly placed.

subfiles.title: Financial position of Japan—additional copy beginning
subfiles.about: Begins another copy of despatch 2038, continuing beyond this section.
subfiles.summary: Opening page of another copy requesting comment on ‘Japan in Suspense.’
